Form simple participial attributes yourself in formal writing.

It's October 2033. Katrin Krüger, the Berliner Zeitung journalist who wrote about “the singing house” in 2031, has published a follow-up. Lena reads the article in the café. Andrei doesn't understand the first sentence.
Listen: “The pianist Margarete Hoffmann, born in Berlin in 1936, who during the war played in an air-raid shelter for frightened children, today teaches two pupils.”
Wait. Is that one sentence? It's twenty words before the verb comes!
It's a participial attribute. Typical of newspapers. You have to read it from the end. Who teaches? The pianist. Which pianist? The one born and who played.
So: the pianist, who was born in Berlin in 1936 and who played in the cellar for children during the war, today teaches two pupils.
Exactly. And further on: “One of the two pupils she teaches free of charge is nine-year-old Elif Yilmaz.”
“Die von ihr unterrichteten Schülerinnen” – the pupils who are taught by her. Partizip II, so passive.
You learn fast. And the other pupil is Elif's mother. Here: “Ayşe Yilmaz, who has dreamt of a piano since she was a child”.
Partizip I: träumend. Ayşe, who has dreamt of a piano since childhood. Active and simultaneous.
And now the most beautiful sentence. About us: “The café run by Lena Brandt and named after her late grandmother has long since become the living room of the whole street.”
The café which is run by Lena Brandt and which bears the name of her grandmother… That's lovely. But why doesn't she write it more simply?

Because she's a real journalist. And because Grandma would have loved this kind of German. She always used to say: a good sentence is like a train. You have to wait until the last carriage has passed.
1. What an extended participial attribute is
Instead of a relative clause AFTER the noun, written German puts all the information BEFORE the noun, between the article and the noun, with the participle at the end, declined like an adjective:
das Café, das von Lena geführt wird
die Frau, die im Keller spielte
der Saal, der im Krieg zerstört wurde
How to recognise it: you see an article (der/die/das/ein) and its noun comes much later; before the noun there is a word in -end- or a participle with an adjective ending.
die spielende Pianistin = who is playing
das gegründete Café = which was founded
der angekommene Zug = which has arrived
Partizip I is always ACTIVE: “die lachenden Kinder” = the children who are laughing. Partizip II of transitive verbs is PASSIVE: “die gekochten Kartoffeln” = the potatoes that have been boiled.
Example: “Die 1936 in Berlin geborene Pianistin unterrichtet zwei Schülerinnen.”
find the article and its noun
find the participle in front of the noun
move the rest into the relative clause, verb at the end

Partizip I → the verb in the tense of the main clause, active: “die spielenden Kinder” → “die Kinder, die spielen”. Transitive Partizip II → passive: “das reparierte Auto” → “das Auto, das repariert wurde”.

At B2 you mainly need to UNDERSTAND it (press, academic texts, documents). In formal writing you can use short attributes: “die geplante Reise”, “das vor kurzem eröffnete Café”, “der von uns vorgeschlagene Termin”. In speech long attributes are hardly ever used.
The variant with “zu”: “die zu erledigenden Aufgaben” = the tasks that have to be done (Gerundiv). You'll often come across it in official texts.

Katrin Krüger came to the “Am Kollwitzpark” care home one Wednesday afternoon in October, with a notebook, a small camera and the firm resolution not to cry. Two years earlier she had written the report about “the singing house” on Kastanienallee, the most-read story of the year in her paper. Since then she had received a letter almost every week from readers who wanted to know how it had gone on. With the old tram driver. With the Romanian nurse. With the old pianist on the fourth floor. Now she wanted to find out for herself.

She had spoken to Mara on the phone beforehand, who had described the way to her and warned her: “Mrs Hoffmann doesn't like journalists. She doesn't like photos either. And she doesn't like being pitied at all. But if you sit quietly and listen, she'll tell you more than you can write down.” Katrin Krüger had thirty years of experience as a reporter. She had interviewed ministers and pop stars and a man who had spent forty years in prison innocent. But before this meeting, she admitted later, she had been just as nervous as at her first interview.

Grete received her in the common room, at the piano, in a grey knitted cardigan and with a pair of reading glasses on her nose, which she took off as soon as the journalist came in. “Mrs Krüger,” she said. “Two years ago you wrote that I am an old lady. That's not true. I am a very old lady. Please write it correctly this time.” Katrin Krüger laughed and promised. Then she sat down in a corner, as quietly as possible, and watched.

Friedrich nodded to her from the window, a polite old gentleman in a grey suit, with a newspaper on his knee that he wasn't reading. He told her later that he had been sitting like that every Wednesday for half a year, and that he only brought the newspaper so that it looked as if he had something else to do than listen to his wife. “But that's a lie,” he said. “I have nothing better to do. I've never had anything better to do.”

At four the pupils came. First Elif, with her school bag on her back and a music book under her arm, then her mother, still in her supermarket overall, because she had come straight from work. They greeted Grete with a handshake, as Grete demanded, and Friedrich, who was sitting in his armchair by the window, with a wave. Then the lesson began. First scales, ten minutes, slowly, over and over again. “A pianist who doesn't practise scales,” Grete used to say, “is like a cook who won't peel potatoes. She'll never cook anything good.”
Out in the corridor you could hear the clatter of dishes and the soft laughter of the carers, who looked forward to this afternoon every week just as much as the residents.

Ayşe played first. She played a simple piece by Schumann, “Of Foreign Lands and Peoples”, which Grete had chosen for her because she thought the title fitted. Ayşe played slowly, very slowly, with the tip of her tongue between her lips, and twice she got stuck and had to start again from the beginning. Grete didn't interrupt her. Only when the piece was over did she say: “Good. In the third line you play too fast, because you're afraid of the difficult passage. Play more slowly, then the fear goes away. The passage stays difficult. But the fear goes away.”

Katrin Krüger wrote as fast as she could. She wrote about nine-year-old Elif, who practised with incredible seriousness and frowned at every wrong note, just like her teacher. She wrote about forty-year-old Ayşe, visibly tired after eight hours at the supermarket till, but who still played every note with concentration, with hands rougher than her daughter's, but just as careful. And she wrote about ninety-seven-year-old Grete, who could barely be heard when she spoke, but noticed every mistake immediately, who sat next to them on a chair and tapped the beat on her knee with a pencil.
Elif, child. Not so hard. The piano is not an enemy. Imagine a little animal is sleeping under every key and you don't want to wake it. You just want to stroke it.

Elif nodded seriously and played the passage once more, more softly, more carefully. And it sounded different. Warmer. Grete said nothing. But she nodded once, barely visibly, and Elif beamed as if she had won a prize. Katrin Krüger saw it and wrote a sentence that she would later not use in the article, because it seemed too personal to her: “Today I saw an art being passed on from one generation to the next. It took two seconds and consisted of a single nod.”

After the lesson, Katrin Krüger sat down with Grete and Friedrich by the window. She asked her questions, and Grete answered, briefly and clearly, as was her way. Why does she do this, at ninety-seven, without money? “Because as a child I played in the cellar so that the other children wouldn't be afraid. I never stopped. I just changed my audience.” Isn't it tiring? “Of course it's tiring. Life is tiring. But a life in which you pass nothing on is boring. And boredom is far more tiring.”

Friedrich, who had been silent the whole time, suddenly said: “May I say something too? For the paper?” Katrin Krüger nodded, surprised. Friedrich looked out of the window, at Kollwitzpark, where the chestnut leaves were already turning yellow and brown. “Write: Friedrich Mertens, aged ninety-eight, who waited sixty-nine years for the woman of his life, sits by the window every Wednesday and listens. And he is the happiest man in Berlin.” Grete laid her hand on his. “That's a very long participial attribute, Friedrich,” she said. “I know,” he said. “I thought about it for a long time.”

Katrin Krüger laughed, and this time she couldn't hold back her tears, although she had resolved so firmly to. She asked Friedrich what it was like to be together again after so long. Friedrich thought for a long time. Then he said: “You know, when I was young I thought love was something big, something loud. Fireworks. Now I know it's quiet. It's an old woman teaching a nine-year-old girl how to stroke a key. And an old man sitting beside her who can't take his eyes off her.”

The article appeared two weeks later, on a Saturday, on the front page of the Berlin section, with a large photo: three hands on a keyboard, one small, one rough, one very old. The headline read: “Das weitergegebene Lied” (The Song Passed On). Lena bought twenty copies and put them out in the café. Ludwig read the article three times, with a magnifying glass, and underlined all the participial attributes in red pen, as Ingrid used to do with her pupils' essays. There were fourteen. He showed them to Andrei, who by now could turn each of them into a version with a relative clause, and said: “See? German is a difficult language. But once you know it, you can say things with it for which other languages need three sentences.”

In the days after the article, letters came. A great many letters, to the paper, to the care home, to the café. A man from Leipzig wrote that he had learned the piano in the sixties with Margarete Hoffmann, at the music school in Pankow, and that even today, at eighty, he played every evening, thanks to her. A woman from Hamburg sent sheet music, old, yellowed Schumann scores that had belonged to her mother, “for little Elif”. And a piano dealer from Charlottenburg rang the café and asked whether the Yilmaz family had a piano at home. When Lena said no, that she practised on an old electronic organ, the man just said: “Give me the address. I have an instrument here that's waiting for someone.”

At the end of the article there was a sentence that Katrin Krüger had first cut and then put back in after all. It was short, without a single participle. Grete had said it when the journalist was already standing at the door, with her coat over her arm. “Don't write that I'm a heroine. I'm not. I'm just an old woman who doesn't want to stop playing the piano. The heroines are the two who come after a long day to learn.”

A week later, in the Yilmaz family's living room, on the second floor of the house at number thirty-three, right next to Ludwig's house, stood a black second-hand piano, which four men had carried up the stairs on Saturday morning. On the lid was a postcard: “For the music passed on by a great teacher.” Elif sat down in front of it, put her hands on the keys, very carefully, as if a little animal were sleeping underneath, and played her first scale. Her mother stood in the doorway and cried. And the following Wednesday, at the care home, Grete said just one word when Elif told her. It wasn't a participle. It was: “Finally.”
